title: How Marisa Peer Built a $20M Coaching Business
overview: In this conversation, Vishen Lakhiani sat down with therapist and author Marisa Peer to unpack how a one-on-one therapy practice became a global training organisation with 20,000 certified therapists. You saw the actual business model, from a free masterclass and a $199 programme through to a $15,000 year-long certification, and how each piece feeds the next. Marisa then turned to the inner game: why 'I'm not enough' is the belief that stops most experts, and the simple steps she uses to dissolve it.
key_ideas: Marisa runs four businesses: training therapists in her method (her main business, with 20,000 therapists trained worldwide), speaking internationally, writing books, and still seeing a small number of clients.

The Mindvalley partnership began over dinner in Mexico after Marisa's husband John introduced her to Vishen. Vishen put her on stage, she was voted best speaker, and in 2015 they published Uncompromised Life, sold through a free 90-minute masterclass; it launched at around $1 to 2 million and was scaled with advertising to about $15 million. Her school opened in November of the same year, and many of its first students came from the Mindvalley audience.

Your message matters more than your credentials. Traditional therapy's message is 'bring me your pain every week for years and the relationship will heal you'. Marisa replaced it with 'bring me your pain and I'll fix you in an hour', and every business with an emotive message does better than one without.
Phraseology: Marisa did not call her work hypnotherapy, she coined RTT, Rapid Transformational Therapy. Great experts coin their own word, and it becomes part of their authority.

The flywheel: leads arrive through a free masterclass, buy a $199 programme, are retargeted with ads, take a quiz on Marisa's site, receive a PDF about becoming an RTT therapist, and enrol in the $15,000 certification that takes nine months to a year. Every graduate then spreads the brand further.

Ask 'What do I require, and what does what I require require of me?' Marisa did not need to write a book, she needed a bestselling book, which required cold-calling magazines and learning to speak on stage. Then do it, even if you do not want to.

Self-doubt is learned, not innate, and it comes down to whether your brain feels safe, so feed it evidence that you are safe to show up, sell and be seen. The biggest belief holding experts back is 'I'm not enough', and most people also quit too early: about 80% want to write a book, 18% do, and under a quarter of one percent ever make money from it, because selling a book is more work than writing it and people expect instant success.

Find your edge by looking at someone good and noticing what they do not do. Marisa spotted that Joe Dispenza did not help Steven Bartlett with his sugar habit on air, offered to hypnotise Steven on his show, and the episode got around 2.5 million views.

dialogue.speaker: Vishen Lakhiani
dialogue.text: Marisa has a hypnotherapy school that teaches her method, RTT, and it does tens of millions a year certifying therapists. She is one of the most successful author brands I know, and Mindvalley had a big part in helping her get to that level. Marisa, tell us about your business and what you do.

dialogue.speaker: Marisa Peer
dialogue.text: Well, I do four things. My real business is training people to be phenomenal therapists. I think the old therapy model is dated, so I have a method, and I've trained 20,000 therapists all over the world. My second business is speaking all over the world, the third is writing books, and the fourth is that I still see clients, not many, but some.

dialogue.speaker: Vishen Lakhiani
dialogue.text: But when you started out, you were basically doing one-on-one, so can I share the story of how we met? Marisa would never attend my event, but her husband John loved Mindvalley events, and on the last day of an event in Mexico he found me in the lobby and said, 'Vishen, have you met my wife? She's one of the top therapists in England, come join us for dinner,' and over dinner I learned you'd been voted number one therapist in Tatler. So I put you on stage at the next event, you were voted best speaker, and we published Uncompromised Life together, sold through a masterclass; I launched it at something like one or two million, then we put advertising behind it and scaled it to 15 million. On the back end of that, what happened, because you and John built a huge coaching school?

dialogue.speaker: Marisa Peer
dialogue.text: One-on-one, yes. And we'd already started the school, but it all came out in the same year, 2015. I did my talk for you in September and my school started in November. A lot of the people who came to that school came from Mindvalley, so yes, we built a huge coaching business, and you really helped us get an even bigger name.

dialogue.speaker: Vishen Lakhiani
dialogue.text: Could you explain what the coaching business looked like?

dialogue.speaker: Marisa Peer
dialogue.text: I'd always been a therapist, and 40 years in I love it as much as I did on day one, but people would ring me from Alabama or Sydney wanting to work with someone like me, and there wasn't anyone, because it was my method and I was a bit possessive of it. My husband, who has put talent on stage his whole life, said, 'Darling, you have to teach this method; I'll find the school, the brochure and the clients, you just turn up,' and that is exactly what happened: my first school was at Regent's College in London, and people came from Guam, Australia and New Zealand looking for something fast. The message of therapy is 'bring me your pain every week for several years and the relationship will make you better,' so I wanted a different message: bring me your pain and I'll fix you in an hour, occasionally three sessions. Every business that tells an emotive message does better than one that doesn't.

dialogue.speaker: Vishen Lakhiani
dialogue.text: Could you give me an idea of what an emotive message is?

dialogue.speaker: Marisa Peer
dialogue.text: AT&T did it with E.T. and 'phone home' (when did you last phone home, while your mother sits on the sofa worried?), and MasterCard did it with Priceless; it's something emotional that tugs at your heartstrings. To be different you also have to be brave enough to put your head above the parapet: somebody wrote to me saying, 'How dare you call your business rapid? The word rapid should never go in front of therapy,' and when I asked why, the answer was 'just because,' which isn't true. We all have a gift, and you're put on the planet to find your gift, perfect your gift and share it with the world.

dialogue.speaker: Vishen Lakhiani
dialogue.text: There were a couple of things Marisa did from a marketing perspective that were really useful. One is what I call phraseology: everyone else calls it hypnotherapy, but Marisa coined her own phrase, RTT, Rapid Transformational Therapy, and great experts coin their own word. The second is that she had a front end and a back end: leads come in through a free 90-minute masterclass into a $199 programme like Uncompromised Life, and then Marisa uses advertising to retarget those people into her coaching school. You go to the website and take a quiz, is that right, then you get a PDF explaining what it means to be an RTT coach, and how much do they pay and how long is the training?

dialogue.speaker: Marisa Peer
dialogue.text: Yes, a quiz. It's $15,000, and the training takes between nine months and a year, depending on how much free time they have.

dialogue.speaker: Vishen Lakhiani
dialogue.text: So $15,000 and a year of training, and at the end she's given that person a beautiful new career. And here's the thing: through the thousands of people she has trained, Marisa is multiplying RTT and making her brand even more known. That's called a flywheel. Every little piece ties into the next, and that's how it becomes a massive business.

dialogue.speaker: Marisa Peer
dialogue.text: That's true, but we also teach marketing. So many people say, 'I'm good at my career, but nobody knows who I am.' Many therapists are empaths, they're good at the job but they don't know what marketing is, so we teach business in a box: who is your customer, what's your market, what's your message, where are they? One thing I learned a long time ago is to ask, what do I require, and what does what I require require of me? When I wrote my book, I didn't require to write a book, I required to write a bestselling book that changed lives, and that required something not easy: cold-calling magazines and learning to be a speaker. Then you do it, even if you don't want to.

dialogue.speaker: Vishen Lakhiani
dialogue.text: My question for you, Marisa, is for the people watching who are experiencing self-doubt or imposter syndrome, that feeling of 'I don't feel worthy of this.' What would be your advice for them? And is there a simple process you could give them to move away from that doubt?

dialogue.speaker: Marisa Peer
dialogue.text: None of you were born with that; there isn't a baby in the world who thinks 'I'm not worthy,' so you learned it somewhere, and if you learnt it, you can unlearn it. Everything comes down to one question, am I safe: when you say 'I'm scared you'll hate my book' you're telling your brain you're not safe and it will move you away, but you can signal 'I'm safe to go on stage, I'm safe to promote my business,' and because the brain always looks for evidence, you give it evidence. The simple process is this: ask yourself whether you like every person in the whole world, and if you don't, why do you care that everybody likes you; then start saying, 'I like myself, I believe in myself, I have a gift and I'm here to share it with the world.' Then define your gift, perfect it and take it to market, knowing your gift is connected to what you loved doing between the ages of 7 and 14, and remember that how you feel comes down to the pictures you make in your head and the words you construct, so use your brilliant brain to talk yourself into it rather than out of it.

dialogue.speaker: Vishen Lakhiani
dialogue.text: What do you think is the biggest belief that holds people back from becoming an authority in their field?

dialogue.speaker: Marisa Peer
dialogue.text: Definitely 'I'm not enough,' 100%. Your brain is not a mystery; the mystery is how you talk to yourself. Muhammad Ali said 'I'm the greatest' when factually he wasn't, but he stated it and embodied it and it became true, and Steven Bartlett says nobody came to his podcast for three years, but he loved it, so he kept going. And here's the thing I find most interesting: most people look at someone good and say, 'I'm going to be like them,' but the trick is to look at someone good and notice what they're not doing. I watched Steven tell Joe Dispenza he couldn't give up sugar and lived in a mess, and Joe just carried on, so I called Steven and said, 'I should come on your show and hypnotise you.' He said yes, it got about 2.5 million views, and that one thing they don't do becomes your edge.

exercises.name: The safety statement
exercises.instructions: Say to yourself, out loud and regularly: 'I like myself. I believe in myself. I have a gift, and I'm here to share it with the world.' Marisa describes this as the first signal to your brain that it is safe to show up.

exercises.name: Trace your gift
exercises.instructions: Write down what you loved doing between the ages of 7 and 14. Marisa says your gift lies directly behind and is connected to those activities.

next_steps: Write your message in one emotive sentence, the way Marisa replaced 'years of weekly sessions' with 'bring me your pain and I'll fix you in an hour', and test whether it tugs at the heart rather than describing a process.
Coin your own phrase for your method (your version of RTT) instead of using the generic name for your field.
Sketch your own front end and back end: what is the free experience, what is the entry-level offer, and what is the deeper programme that leads run into?
Pick one expert you admire, list the one thing they are not doing, and decide how that becomes your edge.
attribution_notes: Every line in this transcript was labelled 'Mindvalley:', so speakers were separated by content. Jason Goldberg's introduction and closing hand-off were identified by his host framing (welcoming Marisa, referencing the chat, handing back to Vishen). Vishen was identified by his questions, his telling of how they met, the Uncompromised Life launch figures and his commentary on phraseology and the flywheel; Marisa by first-person accounts of her therapists, her method, her husband John, her books, her clients and her school's prices. Merged paragraphs were split at the speaker change (for example 'One-on-one, yeah', 'Tatler', 'Yeah, a quiz', 'I think it's $15,000' and 'Between 9 months and a year' are Marisa answering Vishen mid-paragraph). Two passages are less certain: the line 'But I love that expression, take whatever you want, then pay for it' just before Vishen's book-statistics question could belong to either speaker, and a garbled line about the renamed book 'Managing Stress' was left out.
